audits.claim: Entry: the indigenous Sogdian script served letters, documents, and all religious text kinds, while Manichaean and East Syriac script use was tied to religious affiliation; a shared graphic infrastructure does not identify religion.
audits.entry_locator: ## Language family, scripts, and the limits of "lingua franca": table row "Indigenous Sogdian script, ultimately Aramaic-derived"; bullet "Script/use distribution follows RECK §§5, 8, 10–12, 20."
audits.source_locator: Reck 2021, numbered paragraph 5 (HTML full-text galley, id="p5")
audits.source_excerpt: The usage of Manichaean and the East Syriac script was exclusively connected with the religious affiliation of the texts. The indigenous Sogdian script was used for writing all kinds of religious texts and for letters and documents as well.
audits.basis: Paragraph 5 matches the entry's repertoire table row and its limit statement; Reck also adds the hybrid case of Sogdo-Uyghur script for some Christian texts (paragraph 10).
audits.access_limit: HTML galley retrieved in full; the same site's PDF galley (7065) cross-checked for wording; no manuscript facsimiles examined.

audits.claim: Entry margin note: RECK §8 also records fragmentary Brāhmī-script material, so the script repertoire is not exhaustively the three named scripts.
audits.entry_locator: ## Language family, scripts, and the limits of "lingua franca": bullet "This is the main repertoire, not an exhaustive denial of marginal scripts: RECK §8 also notes fragmentary Brāhmī material."
audits.source_locator: Reck 2021, numbered paragraph 8 (id="p8"); the article's script table also lists a Brāhmī script column
audits.source_excerpt: A small amount of very fragmentary texts is written in Brāhmī script. Only a few of them have been identified as yet.
audits.basis: Verbatim match to the entry's parenthetical claim, including its hedging (very fragmentary, few identified).
audits.access_limit: HTML galley retrieved in full; no Brāhmī fragment images or editions inspected.

audits.claim: Entry: Sogdian's lingua-franca role means manuscript language/script alone cannot identify a writer's ethnicity, because Sogdian texts and scripts also served Uyghur communities (RECK §§3, 5, 20–21).
audits.entry_locator: ## Language family, scripts, and the limits of "lingua franca": bullet "RECK §§3, 5, 20–21 supplies a complementary test…"
audits.source_locator: Reck 2021, numbered paragraph 21 (id="p21"); paragraph 3 states the complementary lingua-franca problem
audits.source_excerpt: But the colophons mostly list Old Uyghur names or Sogdian and Uyghur names side by side. So the question of who wrote these texts, Uyghurs or Sogdians, cannot be answered with certainty.
audits.basis: Paragraph 21 gives the entry's exact caution; paragraph 3 independently notes that Sogdian's lingua-franca role makes Sogdian-authored and other-authored (mainly Uyghur) textual evidence hard to distinguish.
audits.access_limit: HTML galley retrieved in full; the underlying manuscript colophons and catalogues not consulted.

audits.claim: Entry: British Library Or.8212/81 preserves a Sogdian heroic episode about Rustam, and the episode itself does not occur in the Persian Šāhnāma (myth–language coupling: shared hero, no fixed plot or textual original).
audits.entry_locator: ## Pantheon, heroic narrative, and symbol grammar: table row "Rustam narrative"
audits.source_locator: Reck 2021, numbered paragraph 15 (id="p15")
audits.source_excerpt: Or. 8212/81 (Ch. 00349), written in the same distinctive handwriting, contains an episode about Rustam, one of the most important heroes of the Šāhnāma ... Although the episode itself does not occur in the Šāhnāma
audits.basis: Verbatim support for both halves of the entry's row, including the shelfmark. Reck adds that Persian words in the text suggest a lost Middle Persian or New Persian original, which supports the entry's instruction not to backdate Ferdowsi's compilation.
audits.access_limit: HTML galley retrieved in full; Sims-Williams 1976, Indo-Iranian Journal 18: 54–61 (Frag. 13), the underlying edition, was not retrieved.

audits.claim: Entry: a Manichaean text may name Zarathuštra and reuse Zoroastrian vocabulary without becoming a Zoroastrian text (identification trap).
audits.entry_locator: ## Religious multilingualism: institutions, not one blended creed: bullet "Concrete identification trap…"
audits.source_locator: Reck 2021, numbered paragraph 15 (id="p15")
audits.source_excerpt: So another Manichaean text, the so-called Zarathuštra fragment, published by Walter B. Henning, uses the person of Zarathuštra as a representative apostle ... But these are no Zoroastrian materials, but Manichaean ones.
audits.basis: Direct statement of the trap; the entry's recasting as a design caution adds no new factual claim.
audits.access_limit: HTML galley retrieved in full; Henning 1934 and the fragment itself not consulted.

audits.claim: Entry: the religious program of Wirkak's funerary monument is contested — Gulácsi and BeDuhn (2012) Zoroastrian reading versus de la Vaissière's later Manichaean-leaning reading (RECK §14); do not settle by calling every image syncretic.
audits.entry_locator: ## Religious multilingualism: institutions, not one blended creed: bullet "**Contested:** the religious program of Wirkak's funerary monument…"
audits.source_locator: Reck 2021, numbered paragraph 14 (id="p14"); the paragraph's citations name Gulácsi and BeDuhn 2012 and De la Vaissière 2019
audits.source_excerpt: Gulácsi ... BeDuhn disproved the first Manichaean identifications, and stress the clear Zoroastrian ... character of the representations of death and afterlife ... de la Vaissière identified, in a more recent article, topics like Mani as Maitreya stopping hunting
audits.basis: The paragraph sets the two readings against each other exactly as the entry states, including the two named publications (Bulletin of the Asia Institute 26 and 29).
audits.access_limit: HTML galley retrieved in full; the two competing articles themselves are paywalled/print and were not retrieved, so only Reck's summary of the dispute was checked.

audits.claim: Entry: Parthian/Middle Persian Manichaean hymns could be transcribed into Sogdian script rather than translated, separating script accessibility from semantic comprehension (RECK §§12, 20).
audits.entry_locator: ## Religious multilingualism: institutions, not one blended creed: bullet "Concrete multilingual case: Parthian/Middle Persian hymns…"
audits.source_locator: Reck 2021, numbered paragraph 20 (id="p20"); paragraph 12 states the same practice with the church-language frame
audits.source_excerpt: The hymns are mostly Parthian. They have not been translated into Sogdian but transcribed into the Sogdian script, so that people who were not able to read the Manichaean script anymore, could nevertheless read the hymns.
audits.basis: Verbatim match; paragraph 12 independently repeats the transcription-into-Sogdian-script practice for Parthian and Middle Persian hymns.
audits.access_limit: HTML galley retrieved in full; the cited hymn editions not consulted.

audits.claim: Entry: Bulayık Christian material includes Syriac, Sogdian, Uyghur, and New Persian, and Sogdian New Testament translations depend on the Syriac Peshitta, not a presumed direct Greek translation (RECK §§10–11).
audits.entry_locator: ## Religious multilingualism: institutions, not one blended creed: bullet "Concrete Christian case: Bulayık material…"
audits.source_locator: Reck 2021, numbered paragraph 10 (id="p10"); paragraph 11 gives the Syriac ecclesiastical-language frame
audits.source_excerpt: The Christian community from Bulayık kept and produced texts in Syriac, Sogdian, Uyghur, and in New Persian as well. ... Parts of Sogdian translations of the New Testament are preserved. They are based on the Syriac Peshitta version
audits.basis: Both components match verbatim, including the Peshitta dependency that the entry contrasts with a direct Greek route.
audits.access_limit: HTML galley retrieved in full; Sims-Williams 2009/2014 editions behind the statements were not retrieved.

audits.claim: Entry: much surviving Sogdian Buddhist literature is translated mostly from Chinese versions, and other transmission relationships occur — translation can move back westward from Chinese, not only eastward from India (RECK §9).
audits.entry_locator: ## Religious multilingualism: institutions, not one blended creed: table row "Buddhist"
audits.source_locator: Reck 2021, numbered paragraph 9 (id="p9")
audits.source_excerpt: most of the texts found in Central Asia are later translations either from an unknown language or Tocharian, but mostly from Chinese versions
audits.basis: Supports the row's Chinese-source direction and its allowance for other affiliations (unknown language, Tocharian); Reck also records Yoshida's "colonial" description of Sogdian Buddhism.
audits.access_limit: HTML galley retrieved in full; individual Buddhist text editions not consulted.

audits.claim: Entry era table: the major surviving Turfan religious-manuscript setting is the eighth to eleventh centuries CE.
audits.entry_locator: ## Era staging: table row "Eighth–eleventh centuries, Turfan"
audits.source_locator: Article abstract on the article landing page; the galley date-range for the fragment corpus
audits.source_excerpt: The fragments represent parts of the literature of Christian, Manichaean and Buddhist communities in Turfan from the eighth to eleventh century CE.
audits.basis: The abstract's date range matches the entry's era row; paragraph 5 records the same corpus as the Berlin Turfan collection's catalogued Sogdian material.
audits.access_limit: Abstract retrieved on the landing page; the abstract is the publisher's own summary, not an independent re-dating.

audits.claim: Entry: local cults with Zoroastrian affinities are chiefly reconstructed from material evidence with a comparatively thin textual base, treated through the polis-religion model (POLIS via RECK §4).
audits.entry_locator: ## Religious multilingualism: table row "Local cults with Zoroastrian affinities"; bullet "**Named framework—polis religion**"
audits.source_locator: Reck 2021, numbered paragraph 4 (id="p4")
audits.source_excerpt: The religion of the Sogdians in their homeland is described as a kind of “polis religion” similar to the situation in the Classical Greece ... but the textual base is very thin
audits.basis: Paragraph 4 supplies both halves: the polis-religion attribution (citing Shenkar 2017) and the thin textual base with material evidence dominant; the entry's "heuristic, not Greek origin" gloss is consistent with Reck's phrasing.
audits.access_limit: HTML galley retrieved in full; Shenkar 2017 itself (Journal Asiatique 305.2) not retrieved.

audits.claim: Entry: the Ancient Letters were recovered by Aurel Stein in 1907 near Dunhuang, and the introduction favours a date around 313–314 CE while acknowledging a history of dating controversy.
audits.entry_locator: ## Letter case studies: institutions visible at sentence scale: bullet "The Ancient Letters were recovered by Aurel Stein in 1907…"
audits.source_locator: Waugh introduction, second paragraph (Silk Road Seattle page, Sims-Williams translations)
audits.source_excerpt: five nearly complete letters, discovered in 1907 by the famous British archaeologist Aurel Stein in a Chinese watch tower just west of the Jade Gate ... the most persuasive arguments ... point to 313 (-314) C.E.
audits.basis: The introduction states the 1907 Stein find, the locate-watch-tower context, and the 313 (-314) CE preference with the dating controversy caveat; it adds the ~90 km-west-of-Dunhuang detail the entry compresses to "near Dunhuang".
audits.access_limit: Introduction and translations retrieved in full; page encoding glitches (e.g. Farnkhund’s rendered with a replacement character) were normalised; the Sogdian text itself was not read.

audits.claim: Entry Letter 1 row: Miwnay lacks clothing and money, seeks help from relatives and a councillor, and reports a priest's charity with an offered camel and escort.
audits.entry_locator: ## Letter case studies: table row "Letter 1: Miwnay → her mother Chatis"
audits.source_locator: Translation of Sogdian Ancient Letter No. 1, recto (Sims-Williams 2004)
audits.source_excerpt: I live wretchedly, without clothing, without money; I ask for a loan, but no-one consents to give me one, so I depend on charity from the priest.
audits.basis: Recto also records the councillor Sagharak, Artivan, and the priest's offer ("I will give you a camel, and a man should go with you"), matching the row's full inventory; AL treats letters 1 and 3 as the "lady in distress" pair.
audits.access_limit: English translation only; square-bracketed restorations and bracketed query marks in AL were not independently collated against the Sogdian.

audits.claim: Entry Letter 3 row: repeated unanswered letters, blocked departure, and Shayn's marginal report that mother and daughter became servants of the Chinese because of Farnkhund's debts.
audits.entry_locator: ## Letter case studies: table row "Letter 3: Miwnay → husband Nanai-dhat; marginal message from daughter Shayn"
audits.source_locator: Translation of Sogdian Ancient Letter No. 3, recto and margin (Sims-Williams 2004)
audits.source_excerpt: Again and again I send you a letter, (but) I do not receive a (single) letter from you ... Because of Farnkhund’s debts we have become the servants of the Chinese, I together with (my) mother.
audits.basis: Both halves match verbatim; the recto is signed "Sent by (your) servant Miwnay" while the verso/margin headers name daughter Shayn, matching the entry's attribution split between main letter and marginal message.
audits.access_limit: English translation only; the entry's advice to distinguish rhetorical "servant" language from actual debt subordination remains an interpretive caution, not a source statement.

audits.claim: Entry Letter 5 row: isolation in Guzang, disrupted departure, stocks including pepper and "white", and a dispute over silver actually received and weighed.
audits.entry_locator: ## Letter case studies: table row "Letter 5: Fri-khwataw → chief merchant Aspandhat"
audits.source_locator: Translation of Sogdian Ancient Letter No. 5, recto (Sims-Williams 2004)
audits.source_excerpt: In Guzang (there are) 4 bundles of "white" for dispatch, and 2,500 (measures of)(?) pepper for dispatch ... He gave me the silver, and I weighed it, and (there were only) four and a half staters altogether.
audits.basis: The recto also states "I have become isolated, and, behold, I stay here in Guzang and I do not go hither (and) thither", matching the isolation/disrupted-departure row; the weighing dispute against a claimed twenty staters follows.
audits.access_limit: English translation only; quantities and the prickly prasthaka units carry AL's own query marks, so no metrology is asserted here.

audits.claim: Entry naming bullet: AL's actual name chain — Varzakk, son of Nanai-thvar, of the Kanakk family; sender Nanai-vandak addresses the recipient as "lord" and describes himself as "servant".
audits.entry_locator: ## Naming practices and addressable identities: first bullet ("Use AL's actual name chains before extrapolating…")
audits.source_locator: Envelope, verso address, and recto opening of Sogdian Ancient Letter No. 2 (Sims-Williams 2004)
audits.source_excerpt: To the noble lord Varzakk (son of) Nanai-thvar (of the family) Kanakk, 1,000 (and) 10,000 (times) blessing (and) homage on bended knee, as is offered to the gods, sent by his servant Nanai-vandak.
audits.basis: Exact match to the entry's name chain; the envelope and verso repeat the address formula, supporting the entry's point that the envelope participates in delivery and social authentication.
audits.access_limit: English translation only; the entry's separate caution on -vandak's devotional value versus NAMES (Lurje 2010) was not rechecked and remains (to-verify).

audits.claim: Entry chronicle caution: Letter 2's "Huns" belongs to an early-fourth-century Chinese crisis (Luoyang's destruction in 311 CE) and a particular translated ethnonym that cannot simply identify every later European group called Hun.
audits.entry_locator: ## Letter case studies: bullet "**Chronicle caution:** Letter 2's "Huns"…"
audits.source_locator: Translation of Sogdian Ancient Letter No. 2, recto; Waugh introduction, third paragraph ("the latter occurred in 311 CE")
audits.source_excerpt: Luoyang (is) no more, Ye (is) no more! ... these (same) Huns [who] yesterday were the emperor's (subjects)!
audits.basis: The letter's Huns are embedded in the 311 CE Luoyang/Ye crisis as the introduction states, so the entry's warning against equating them with later European Huns is consistent with the source's own framing (the translation prints the ethnonym with a question mark).
audits.access_limit: English translation only; the written problem of the Sogdian/Chinese ethnonym was not pursued into secondary literature.

audits.claim: Entry material caution: "white" in Letter 5 is interpreted as probably white lead in AL's introduction, and other commodity names and units remain unresolved rather than silently resolved.
audits.entry_locator: ## Letter case studies: bullet "**Material caution:** "white" in Letter 5…"
audits.source_locator: Waugh introduction, product list paragraph
audits.source_excerpt: and "white" (probably white lead powder, a valuable commodity used in cosmetics and drugs). Unfortunately the meaning of some terms for other products is not known.
audits.basis: Verbatim support for both the probable white-lead identification and the entry's insistence on retained uncertainty for other commodity terms.
audits.access_limit: English introduction only; no commodity study or archaeometric literature consulted.

audits.claim: Entry (flagged, load-bearing): DRESS's section on images of "Others" says Sogdian/Tokharistian merchant costume is poorly known, so a rich sartorial repertoire is not a securely reconstructed caravan uniform.
audits.entry_locator: ## Costume and material signatures: bullet "Especially important: DRESS's section on images of "Others"…"
audits.source_locator: Yatsenko 2003, section "Sogdians in the art of other countries: the images of the 'Others'", final paragraph
audits.source_excerpt: The costume of Sogdian and Tokharistian merchants is practically neither known as well (though some of participants of scenes in Penjikent paintings are at times called «feasting merchants»).
audits.basis: Verbatim match — the source is if anything stronger than the entry's "poorly known" phrasing, and its few "merchant" attributions are explicitly hedged ("at times called").
audits.access_limit: Web-festschrift page (updated 2004) retrieved in full; its illustrations/plates are not served on the page, so the visual corpus could not be inspected directly.

audits.claim: Entry: avoid "Chinese-produced image = exact ethnographic portrait"; DRESS itself disputes several figure identifications.
audits.entry_locator: ## Costume and material signatures: bullet "Avoid "silk = everyone's daily clothing"… DRESS itself disputes several figure identifications."
audits.source_locator: Yatsenko 2003, section "Sogdians in the art of other countries: the images of the 'Others'", opening paragraph
audits.source_excerpt: efforts of different authors to identify these figurines (very often not accompanied by any argumentation) cannot be called successful on the whole
audits.basis: The source's own methodological complaint matches the entry's caution; Yatsenko then offers his own probability-graded attributions, which supports the entry's rule to label attribution certainty per figure.
audits.access_limit: Text retrieved in full; the named museum figurines (e.g. Museum für Völkerkunde, Berlin) were not inspected as objects.

audits.claim: Entry: DRESS's main evidence is painting and terracotta, with scarcer actual clothing remains, including Mount Mug textiles.
audits.entry_locator: ## Costume and material signatures: first bullet ("DRESS's main evidence is painting and terracotta…")
audits.source_locator: Yatsenko 2003, subsection on written sources and real clothing remnants (paragraph naming the mountain castle of Devashtich)
audits.source_excerpt: Of real clothing remnants of the articles made of fabrics and woven of cotton thread from the mountain castle of the ruler Devashtich (the bound of the 7th - 8th cc.) on the mountain Mug are especially valuable
audits.basis: The paragraph confirms that real clothing remnants exist but are singled out as exceptionally valuable; note the fabrics are described as cotton-thread articles, so these objects do not license a "silk" everyday-clothing inference either.
audits.access_limit: Text retrieved in full; no object catalogue or textile analysis of the Mount Mug finds was retrieved.

audits.claim: Entry: patterned silks and pearl medallions belong to the visual repertoire, and an imported textile can become a locally cut coat (track cloth production, garment construction, ownership, and repair separately).
audits.entry_locator: ## Costume and material signatures: table row "Fabric pattern and lining"; bullet "**Cosmopolitanism mechanism:**"
audits.source_locator: Yatsenko 2003, subsection "Color Range"
audits.source_excerpt: The edging of expensive polychromic imported silk with flower pattern or medallions of pearls (the latter often being white with red rimming) played a very important role in general color range.
audits.basis: Supports both the pearl-medallion/patterned-silk repertoire row and the entry's imported-cloth-versus-local-garment distinction: the source frames such silk as imported and used as edging on depicted garments.
audits.access_limit: Text retrieved in full; the origin of the depicted silks (Sogdian, Chinese, or other) is not established by this passage and remains outside the check.

audits.claim: Entry era table: DRESS proposes an earlier "Hephthalite" (5th–6th c.) and a later "Turkic" (7th–early 8th c.) costume phase, and the two-period scheme is one author's reconstruction rather than a universal ladder.
audits.entry_locator: ## Era staging: table rows "Fifth–sixth centuries, homeland dress corpus" and "Seventh–early eighth centuries, homeland"; bullet "DRESS's two-period scheme…"
audits.source_locator: Yatsenko 2003, Abstract, first sentence
audits.source_excerpt: Two periods in the history of the Sogdian costume can be singled out: Heptalitian (5th -6th cc.) and Turcic (7th - the beg. of the 8th c.).
audits.basis: The phase boundary and dates match the entry's two era rows; the source's own spellings are Heptalitian/Turcic, which the entry normalises to Hephthalite/Turkic — a transliteration variance, not a factual difference.
audits.access_limit: Abstract and body text retrieved in full; the article states its material derives from the author's 2002 dissertation, which was not retrieved.

audits.claim: Entry costume table: one- and two-lapel open-front coats; women's dress distinguished from performers' ensembles; trousers with differentiated colours — no single uniform silhouette for either sex.
audits.entry_locator: ## Costume and material signatures: table rows "Outer garment", "Trousers and footwear", "Women's dress"
audits.source_locator: Yatsenko 2003, Abstract (garment summary)
audits.source_excerpt: Grown-up men's kaftans usually had two lapels in Turcic manner, but youths sometimes had only one ... female-dancers often wore short dresses accomplished with trousers. The upper part of the trouser-legs ... were of different color.
audits.basis: All three table elements are traceable to the abstract's summary, including the one-lapel youth variant that the entry warns against using as an infallible ethnicity test.
audits.access_limit: Summary-level support only: the article's plate-by-plate arguments were not re-examined figure by figure.

audits.claim: Entry LOANS rows (p. 40): Mongolian üsüg "letter, writing" via a Turkic term for written character/letter/syllable, and küji "incense" through Turkic, both discussed among Sogdian-origin cultural words.
audits.entry_locator: ## Sogdian loan layers in Turkic and Mongolian: table rows "Scribal technique" and "Ritual commodity"
audits.source_locator: Clark 1980, p. 40 (OCR running heads place the passage between the p. 40 and p. 41 head lines)
audits.source_excerpt: Mongol has also borrowed a few cultural words which contained in Old Turkic the foreign sound i, indicative of a Sogdian origin ... küß “incense” ... üaüg/üjäg “letter, writing” Tü üküklüiek “written character, letter, syllable”
audits.basis: Both words appear in the source's Sogdian-indicative cultural-word list on p. 40, exactly as the entry's two rows claim; the entry's hedging ("discussed among Sogdian-origin cultural words") matches Clark's "indicative of a Sogdian origin".
audits.access_limit: OCR layer of the altaica.ru scan; OCR mangles diacritics (küji printed as küß, üsüg as üaüg/üjäg, č as b), so no donor spelling or sound law is re-derived from this retrieval, consistent with the entry's own caveat. Page numbers inferred from OCR running heads.

audits.claim: Entry LOANS row (p. 43): Mongolian bačaγ/mačaγ "fast" via a Turkic noun related to a Sogdian-derived verb — a recipient-language derivation between two borrowing events.
audits.entry_locator: ## Sogdian loan layers in Turkic and Mongolian: table row "Ascetic practice"
audits.source_locator: Clark 1980, p. 43 (OCR running head line "TURKIC LOANWORDS IN MONGOL 43")
audits.source_excerpt: babaγ/mabaγ “fast” «- Tü babaγ id. < baba- “to fast” «- Sogdian
audits.basis: The chain (Sogdian → Turkic verb/noun → Mongol) matches the entry's row. The OCR prints the č as b, so the printed forms are presumably bačaγ/mačaγ and bača-, as the entry already warns; the derivation step indicated by "id. < …" is present in the source.
audits.access_limit: OCR damage to the affricate (č printed as b); no clean edition or dictionary (e.g. ED) consulted to restore the exact donor spellings.

audits.claim: Entry LOANS rows (p. 43): Sanskrit śrāmaṇerī through Sogdian and Turkic behind Mongolian "nun" terminology, and Sanskrit upāsikā through Sogdian and Turkic behind Mongolian "lay woman" terminology.
audits.entry_locator: ## Sogdian loan layers in Turkic and Mongolian: table rows "Buddhist monastic office" and "Buddhist lay affiliation"
audits.source_locator: Clark 1980, p. 43 (adjacent entries in the Turkic-final-b assimilation list)
audits.source_excerpt: simnanba ... “nun” «- Tü bimnanb id. «- Sogdian šmn'nb «- Skt bramaneri ... ubasanba “lay woman” «- Tü upasanb id. «- Sogdian ’wp'e’nb «- Skt upāsikā (ATG 378; DTS 613)
audits.basis: Both entries show the full four-stage chain the entry claims (Sanskrit → Sogdian → Turkic → Mongol), with the same institutional glosses ("nun", "lay woman"); the entry's distinction between monastic and household terms is present in the source pair.
audits.access_limit: OCR damage to Sogdian/Sanskrit diacritics (e.g. bramaneri for śrāmaṇerī); Mongol variant sets are printed only in the damaged OCR forms, so the entry's "(to-verify) in clean editions" marker remains justified.

audits.claim: Entry caution: do not automatically label bäg/beg or qatun/khātūn securely Sogdian on resemblance or popular etymology alone; donor direction, form, and chronology are (to-verify).
audits.entry_locator: ## Sogdian loan layers in Turkic and Mongolian: bullet "Court titles and commercial words need separate dossiers…"
audits.source_locator: Clark 1980, p. 41 (Mongolian qatun in the "Treatment of Turkic i" list of Turkic loans)
audits.source_excerpt: qatun “principal or first wife of a khan”
audits.basis: Clark lists Mongolian qatun among Turkic loanwords with a Turkic source word, and nowhere in the retrieved pp. 40–43 assigns it a Sogdian donor — consistent with the entry's instruction to keep the Sogdian direction unverified rather than assumed.
audits.access_limit: Absence of a Sogdian assignment in the retrieved page range is not proof that no Sogdian etymology exists; the entry's (to-verify) status is therefore preserved, not resolved. OCR damage affects the Turkic comparandum printed on the same line.

audits.source_locator: no passage retrieved (Encyclopaedia Iranica article page refused the fetch; the entry's PANTHEON source, Grenet 2015 in the Wiley Blackwell Companion, and POLIS are print/paywalled)

audits.claim: Entry: Sogdian is an Indo-European → Indo-Iranian → Iranian language, not Turkic, Mongolic, or a dialect of Chinese (LANGUAGE: Sims-Williams 1989); "Middle Iranian" is a classification, not a single-politics or single-dialect claim.
audits.entry_locator: ## Language family, scripts, and the limits of "lingua franca": first two bullets
audits.source_locator: Waugh introduction, first paragraph
audits.source_excerpt: The Sogdians, a people of Iranian origin, were important in the commerce of the Silk Road between the fourth and ninth centuries CE.
audits.basis: The institutional source independently frames Sogdians as Iranian; Reck's paragraph 21 separately keeps Sogdian and Old Uyghur apart as different languages, which rules out the Turkic/Mongolic misclassifications the entry guards against.
audits.access_limit: Only the "Iranian, not Turkic" component is directly retrieved. The finer "conventionally classed as Eastern Iranian" sub-classification rests on Sims-Williams 1989 (print, not retrieved; iranicaonline 403), so that sub-claim remains unchecked rather than promoted.
